Henri Poincaré. A French mathematician, theoretical physicist, and philosopher of science from eighteen fifty-four to nineteen twelve, often described as the last universalist in mathematics. He founded algebraic topology, made seminal contributions to the three-body problem that laid the groundwork for modern chaos theory, and independently developed concepts of special relativity. His most famous conjecture concerning the topology of three-spheres remained unsolved for nearly a century until Grigori Perelman proved it in two thousand three.

He founded algebraic topology by introducing the concept of the fundamental group and homology groups in his paper Analysis Situs. He made seminal contributions to the three-body problem, which revealed that even simple deterministic systems can exhibit chaotic behaviour, effectively founding modern chaos theory. His work showed that predictability has limits, a revolutionary insight.

He formulated the Poincaré conjecture, which asserts that every simply connected, closed three-manifold is homeomorphic to the three-sphere. This conjecture was the only Millennium Prize Problem solved, when Grigori Perelman proved it in two thousand three, nearly a century after it was posed.

He formulated the Poincaré recurrence theorem, which states that certain systems will, after a sufficiently long time, return to a state arbitrarily close to their initial state. Independently, he developed key concepts of special relativity, introducing the Lorentz transformations in their modern form and the Poincaré group. He also proposed the Poincaré half-plane model and disk model, providing concrete realisations of hyperbolic geometry.
